qs.q: A newborn infant is admitted to the nursery with hypothermia. Why are newborns particularly dependent on brown adipose tissue for thermoregulation?
o: Lacking the ability to shiver effectively
Storing no triglycerides within brown fat
Having a small relative body surface area
qs.e: Newborns rely heavily on brown adipose tissue because they lack the ability to shiver effectively. Newborns actually have a large surface area to body mass ratio, which contributes to rapid heat loss.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Thermoregulation maintains core temperature within a narrow range using heat production and loss mechanisms. Failure leads to hypothermia or hyperthermia, each with distinct clinical signs and urgent risks.

sections.p: Core temperature is kept around 36.5‑37.5 °C by coordinated neural and hormonal responses. The hypothalamic preoptic area acts as the thermostat, integrating peripheral and central temperature inputs.
b: Key organs: hypothalamus, skin, brown adipose tissue, skeletal muscle

sections.p: Heat is generated by shivering, non‑shivering thermogenesis (brown fat), and metabolism; heat is lost via radiation, convection, conduction, and evaporation. Vasomotor tone and sweating are the primary effectors.
b: Shivering: rapid muscle contractions increase heat production
Brown fat oxidation: uncoupled mitochondria generate heat without movement
Vasoconstriction reduces cutaneous blood flow, conserving heat

t.b: Does peripheral temperature reflect central set‑point? Low skin temp with normal core suggests peripheral vasoconstriction, not hypothermia.
Is basal metabolic rate elevated? High T3/T4 can augment heat production, relevant in hyperthyroidism.

sections.p: The hypothalamus receives afferent signals from cutaneous thermoreceptors and central thermosensors, then modulates autonomic output and endocrine pathways to adjust heat balance.
b: Cold → sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, shivering, BAT activation
Heat → parasympathetic dominance → vasodilation, sweating, reduced metabolism

t.b: Are sympathetic pathways activated? Elevated norepinephrine supports cold‑stress response.

sections.p: Disruption of any component—sensor, integrator, or effector—produces temperature dysregulation. Common clinical entities are hypothermia, hyperthermia, and fever of unknown origin.
b: Hypothermia: core <35 °C, often from exposure, sepsis, or drugs
Hyperthermia: core >40 °C, from heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Fever: regulated rise due to pyrogens, infection, inflammation

t.b: If thermometer unavailable, assess mental status, skin color, and shivering; treat empirically if high suspicion.

sections.p: Recognizing abnormal thermoregulation directs urgent interventions and clues to underlying disease, especially in low‑resource settings where infections and environmental exposure are common.
b: Heat stroke: rapid cooling prevents organ failure; common in tropical climates
Septic hypothermia: early warming improves outcomes; seen in malaria, TB, HIV
Neonatal hypothermia: brown fat loss and limited shivering require skin‑to‑skin care

t.b: If lab unavailable, use clinical sepsis criteria (tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status).
If unavailable, monitor urine output and CK if possible.

sections.p: Focus on the physiologic loop, key triggers, and emergency management steps.
b: Heat‑stroke treatment: ice‑water immersion 10‑15 min, then evaporative cooling
Hypothermia treatment: passive rewarming + active core warming if severe

whenToSeekHelp: Core temperature >40 °C with altered mental status (heat stroke)
Core temperature <32 °C with bradycardia or hypotension (severe hypothermia)
Rapidly rising fever >39 °C in a patient on antipsychotics (possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

faq.q: Why do newborns rely on brown fat instead of shivering?
faq.a: They lack sufficient muscle mass for shivering; brown fat provides rapid, non‑shivering heat via uncoupled mitochondria.
Fever itself is protective, but very high temperatures (>41 °C) can cause protein denaturation and seizures, especially in children.

faq.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from fever?
faq.a: Heat stroke is an unregulated rise due to environmental overload; fever is a regulated hypothalamic response to pyrogens.

exam: Explain the hypothalamic pathways that trigger shivering and sweating.
